prompt: Which line declares a function taking two `int` parameters called `width` and `height`?
hint: In Go the name comes before its type.

choices.text: `func area(int width, int height) int`
choices.why: That is the C order. Go reads it as two parameters called `int`, of a type called `width` and one called `height`.

choices.text: `func area(width, height int) int`
choices.why: Right. The name comes first, and neighbouring parameters of one type share it.

choices.text: `func area(width: int, height: int) int`
choices.why: That is how Python's type hints and TypeScript write it. Go puts no colon between a name and its type.

choices.text: `func area(int, int width, height) int`
choices.why: Grouping shares one type among the names before it; it does not list the types first and the names after.

prompt: `func area(int width, int height) int` fails with `int redeclared in this block`. Why does the compiler talk about `int` at all?
hint: Read each pair as Go reads it: name, then type.

choices.text: Because `int` is a keyword and cannot appear in a parameter list twice
choices.why: `int` is a predeclared name, not a keyword, which is exactly why it can be used as a parameter's name.

choices.text: Because Go has only one integer type per function
choices.why: A function may take any mix of types; `label` took a `string`, two `int` and a `string`.

choices.text: Each pair declares a parameter named `int`, so the second one is a redeclaration
choices.why: Right. `int width` is a parameter called `int` of a type called `width`; two of them clash, and `width` is undefined.

choices.text: Because the result type `int` repeats a parameter's type
choices.why: Results and parameters may share a type freely: `area(width, height int) int` compiled.

prompt: Go has no default parameter values. How does the `strings` package offer a split with a limit on the number of pieces?
hint: Look at the names `go doc strings` listed.

choices.text: `Split` takes an optional third argument
choices.why: Optional arguments do not exist; `Split` takes exactly `(s, sep string)`.

choices.text: A second `Split` with three parameters overloads the first
choices.why: Two functions with one name in a package are refused: `redeclared in this block`.

choices.text: A separate function with its own name, `SplitN`, that has an `n int` parameter
choices.why: Right. Each variant is its own function, so a call names exactly the code that runs.

choices.text: You pass `-1` to `Split` to mean no limit
choices.why: That confuses the two: `SplitN` takes the count, and `Split` has no parameter to pass it in.

prompt: Two functions named `area` in one package, even with different parameters, stop the build with `area ___ in this block`.
hint: The same word appears when a name is declared twice anywhere.

prompt: `func area(width, height int, unit string) int` never reads `unit`. What happens when you build it?
hint: Lesson 5's rule was about local variables.

choices.text: The build stops with `declared and not used: unit`
choices.why: That rule covers variables declared in a function body; a parameter is part of the signature and is exempt.

choices.text: It builds, and `go vet` says nothing either
choices.why: Right. The parameter list is a contract with the caller, and a signature sometimes has to accept a value it ignores.

choices.text: It builds, but `go vet` reports the unused parameter
choices.why: `go vet && go run .` printed 12 and nothing else: vet had no complaint.

choices.text: It builds only if the parameter is renamed `_`
choices.why: Naming it `_` is allowed and says you ignore it on purpose, but it is not required.

prompt: `divmod` returns `(int, int)`. What does `q := divmod(17, 5)` do?
hint: Count the names on the left and the values on the right.

choices.text: `q` gets the first result, 3, and the remainder is dropped
choices.why: Some languages do that; Go refuses, so a result is never lost without you saying so.

choices.text: It does not compile: one variable but two values
choices.why: Right: `assignment mismatch: 1 variable but divmod returns 2 values`.

choices.text: `q` holds a pair, `(3, 2)`, that can be indexed later
choices.why: Go has no tuples. `(int, int)` is a list of results, not a type a variable can have.

choices.text: `q` gets the last result, 2
choices.why: No result is picked for you, first or last; the assignment is refused.

prompt: `fmt.Println(divmod(17, 5))` prints `3 2`, but `fmt.Println("result:", divmod(17, 5))` does not compile. Why?
hint: When can a multi-result call fill another call's arguments?

choices.text: `Println` cannot print a string and a number in one call
choices.why: It can: `Println` accepts values of any type, mixed freely.

choices.text: The string must come after the call
choices.why: Order is not the issue. Mixed with any other argument, before or after, the call is refused.

choices.text: A multi-result call spreads over arguments only when it is the whole argument list
choices.why: Right. With anything beside it, the compiler wants one value there: `multiple-value … in single-value context`.

choices.text: Two results are joined into a string first, which fails
choices.why: Nothing is joined. The results are separate values, and the error says a single value was expected.

prompt:
What does this print?

```go
n, _ := strconv.Atoi("12a")
fmt.Println(n + 5)
```
hint: What does a failed `Atoi` hand back as its number?

prompt: When is writing `_` for a returned `error` a defensible choice?
hint: Lesson 12 did it once, and this lesson said why that was safe.

choices.text: Whenever the program has been tested and works
choices.why: Tests pass on the input you tried; `"42x"` became 0 without a word, and a test with good input would never see it.

choices.text: Never: the compiler refuses `_` in place of an `error`
choices.why: It accepts it, which is why it needs care: `n, _ := strconv.Atoi("42x")` compiled and printed 1.

choices.text: When the value is printed straight away, so a wrong one shows
choices.why: A failed `Atoi` printed 0, which looks like a perfectly good number; nothing showed.

choices.text: When you know why the failure cannot happen or does not matter
choices.why: Right. `json.Marshal` on a slice of strings is such a case: none of its listed failures applies.

prompt: `divmod` returns `(int, int)`. Which of these lines compile? Choose every one that does.
hint: A blank holds a place; it does not remove one.

choices.why: Compiles: `_` takes the quotient and `r` the remainder.

choices.text: `fmt.Println(divmod(17, 5))`
choices.why: Compiles: the call is the whole argument list, so both results become arguments.
There is no tuple to index: the results are two values, not one value with two parts.

choices.text: `q, r := divmod(17, 5)` followed only by `fmt.Println(q)`
choices.why: `r` is declared and never used, which stops the build: `declared and not used: r`.

prompt: A function `func sign(n int) string` returns `"negative"` inside `if n < 0 { … }` and `"other"` inside `if n >= 0 { … }`, and has nothing after the two `if`. Every integer is covered. What does the compiler say?
hint: Does the check look at values, or at the shape of the code?

choices.text: Nothing: the two conditions cover every `n`, so every path returns
choices.why: True of the values, but the check does not reason about them; it sees an `if` that might not run before the closing brace.

choices.text: `missing return`, at the closing brace
choices.why: Right. The compiler checks the shape of the paths, and after an `if` with no `else` there is a path that falls through.

choices.text: Nothing, and it returns `""` if neither branch runs
choices.why: Go does not supply a zero value for a missing `return`; it refuses to compile.

choices.text: A warning from `go vet`, but the program builds
choices.why: This is the compiler's rule, not vet's, and it is an error: the build stops.

prompt: `func nothing() (n int, s string, err error)` contains only `return`. What does it return?
hint: A named result is a variable.

choices.text: Nothing: a bare `return` in a function with results is an error
choices.why: With named results a bare `return` is legal; it returns what the names hold.

choices.text: `0`, `""` and `nil`, the zero value of each
choices.why: Right. Named results are declared when the function starts and set to their zero values, and it printed `0 "" <nil>`.

choices.text: Undefined values, since nothing assigned them
choices.why: Go has no undefined values; every variable starts at its type's zero, as lesson 6 showed.

choices.text: Only `err`, as `nil`
choices.why: A function returns all its results every time; the caller received three values.

prompt: A `return` with nothing after it, in a function whose results have names, is called a ___ return.
hint: It has two common names in English; either is accepted.

prompt: `port("8080")` declares `n, err := strconv.Atoi(s)` inside an `if`, returns `n, err` explicitly there on failure, and ends with a bare `return`. `go vet` is silent. What does `fmt.Println(port("8080"))` print after `parsed 8080`?
hint: Which `n` does the last `return` see?

choices.why: That is what was meant, and it is why the bug survives review: the 8080 is in the inner `n`, which the last `return` cannot see.
Right. The bare `return` hands back the outer results, which nobody assigned.

choices.text: Nothing: the compiler refuses the bare `return` at the end
choices.why: It refuses a bare `return` only where a result is hidden, inside the `if`; at the end nothing hides them.

choices.text: `8080` followed by an error saying `err` was shadowed
choices.why: Shadowing produces no run-time error; the program ran and printed zero values.

prompt: Why does `strings.Cut` name its results `(before, after string, found bool)` rather than writing `(string, string, bool)`?
hint: Where do you meet that signature first?

choices.text: So the signature in `go doc` says which string is which
choices.why: Right. The names document the order that two results of one type would otherwise hide.

choices.text: Because a function returning three values must name them
choices.why: Names are never required; `divmod` returned two unnamed results and the compiler had no objection.

choices.text: So callers can pick results by name, as in `Cut(s, "=").after`
choices.why: The names belong to the function; a caller receives plain values and names them itself.

choices.text: Named results run faster
choices.why: Nothing in the lesson measured speed; the reason given is the documentation.

prompt:
What does `f()` return?

```go
func f() (n int) {
	defer func() { n *= 2 }()
	return 5
}
```
hint: `return 5` sets `n` first. What runs after that?

prompt: Put in order what happens when `answer()` runs, `func answer() (n int)` with a deferred `n++` and `return 41`.
hint: The deferred function runs between the `return` statement and the caller.
items: the deferred function adds one to `n`

prompt:
What does `g()` return?

```go
func g() int {
	n := 5
	defer func() { n *= 2 }()
	return n
}
```
hint: Is `n` the result here, or a local variable whose value `return` copies?

choices.text: 10, because the deferred function runs before the value leaves
choices.why: It does run, but it doubles a local variable after `return n` already copied 5 into the unnamed result.

choices.text: 5: the deferred call changes a local `n`, not the result
choices.why: Right. Only a named result is a variable a deferred function can reach after `return`; this one has no name.

choices.text: Nothing: `defer` needs a named result to compile
choices.why: `defer` works in any function; only changing the result needs a name.

choices.text: 0, because `defer` resets the result
choices.why: Nothing is reset; `n *= 2` doubles a variable, and the result never sees it.

prompt: A colleague's 40-line function has named results and four bare `return` statements, two inside nested `if` blocks that use `:=`. Which concerns from this lesson apply? Choose every one that does.
hint: Think about the reader, and about shadowing.

choices.text: A reader at a `return` has to scroll up and search the body to know what it returns
choices.why: Yes. The bare form reads well only when the results are visible on the same screen.

choices.text: A `:=` in a block may declare new variables that hide the results
choices.why: Yes. That is the `port` bug: the work landed in inner variables and the caller got zeros.

choices.text: Named results make the function slower than unnamed ones
choices.why: The lesson made no claim about speed, and none of its captures measured one.

choices.text: Go allows at most one bare `return` per function
choices.why: There is no such limit; the rule is about hidden results, not about how many returns there are.
